prompt: A dynamic array adds exactly one hundred slots whenever it is full and copies its existing contents on every resize. Why does this scale worse than multiplying capacity by a fixed factor?

options.text: It wastes an exponentially growing number of empty slots
options.explanation: The fixed number of added slots does not create exponential spare capacity.

options.text: Each new hundred-slot block costs more to allocate by definition
options.explanation: The issue here is repeatedly copying the growing existing contents, not an assumed allocation price.

options.text: A fixed number of appends separates increasingly large copies
options.explanation: Correct. Copy sizes keep growing while the gap between resizes stays fixed, giving quadratic total copying.

options.text: Multiplicative growth guarantees no future resize
options.explanation: It still resizes, but the larger gaps keep total copying linear.

workedExample: After each fixed-increment resize, only another hundred appends fit. The next resize copies a larger existing array. These arithmetic-progression copy sizes have a quadratic total in append count. Multiplicative growth creates proportionally more room and a geometric progression with linear total.

prompt: A stack built on a dynamic array doubles when full and **halves when it becomes half full**. A workload repeatedly pushes and pops one item while the stack holds about 1 million items, and it is mysteriously slow. What is going on?

options.text: Popping is inherently O(n) in dynamic arrays
options.explanation: Popping from the end is O(1) when no resize happens. The problem is the shrink rule, not pop itself.

options.text: Halving at half full means a push/pop pair at the boundary resizes every time, so each operation costs Θ(n)
options.explanation: Correct. Full at capacity k: push doubles to 2k (copy k). Pop leaves it half full, so it halves to k (copy k). The next push doubles again. Every operation copies about a million elements.

options.text: The amortised analysis guarantees O(1), so the slowness must come from elsewhere
options.explanation: The O(1) amortised guarantee depends on the resize policy. With this shrink rule, the guarantee doesn't hold.

options.text: The array should grow by 1.5x rather than 2x
options.explanation: Changing the growth factor doesn't fix it. Any policy that shrinks right at the point it just grew from can thrash.

workedExample: A push from a full state grows the array; the next pop returns it to half full and immediately shrinks it. Repeating the pair triggers full copying on every operation. Shrinking only at a quarter full leaves a substantial gap before the next growth or shrink, restoring the sequence argument under the stated copy model.

prompt: Assume an initially empty array with fixed initial capacity, copying all existing elements whenever it grows. Which append-only growth policies give constant amortised cost? Round capacities upward as needed. Select all that apply.

options.explanation: Correct. Doubling gives linear total copying.
Correct. A fixed factor above one creates proportional spare capacity and keeps total copying linear.
Not constant amortised cost. A fixed increment eventually gives quadratic total copying.

options.text: Multiply capacity by a fixed factor of 1.125, with rounding and a small constant
options.explanation: Correct. A fixed factor above one keeps total copying linear in append count.
Not constant amortised cost. One-slot growth copies every earlier item on each append.

workedExample: For the copy-on-resize model starting empty, a fixed multiplicative growth factor above one produces linear total copying. A fixed number of added slots eventually gives almost no proportional headroom and produces quadratic copying. Integer rounding and fixed minimum capacity do not change these asymptotic distinctions.
